# Embedded skill: sarvam-html-presentation

# Sarvam HTML Presentation Skill

Create one authored HTML deck by **assembling a tested component library, not
by authoring CSS**. The core substrate (`assets/deck-core.css` +
`assets/deck-core.js`) is embedded verbatim and hash-checked; a selected theme
supplies tokens and a small component vocabulary; you supply content and
composition. Your craft goes into the words, the evidence, and the choice of
composition — not into reinventing charts, grids, or type scales.

## Output contract

- One self-contained `.html` file. Only external requests: the theme's Google
Fonts link. Supplied images may remain relative assets.
- Slides are 16:9 CSS containers (`.sheet--slide`); every size derives from
`--fs`/`--sp`/`--pad` in `cqw`, so the deck scales identically in the review
scroll, fullscreen present mode, and print. Never use `px` type sizes,
`vw/vh` units, or media queries inside a sheet.
- Core CSS and JS embedded **verbatim including sentinel comments** — the
validator rejects edited or re-typed cores.
- Charts via the declarative `data-chart` engine. Never hand-author chart SVG.
- Present mode, keyboard/click/swipe navigation, reveal animation,
reduced-motion support, and 1280×720 print come from the core for free.

## Workflow

### 1. Infer the brief

Identify the mode: new deck, source-to-slides, PowerPoint conversion, or
existing-HTML edit. For a new deck, infer audience, outcome, narrative angle,
and evidence depth from the request and material. Do not run a generic
questionnaire — the only required clarification is the template choice below.

- Talk, keynote, pitch → speaker-led, fewer words, bigger claims.
- Report, review, briefing → reading-first, denser evidence.
- No slide count given → use the count the content needs; never pad or cram.

### 2. Choose the look

Read [references/template-index.json](references/template-index.json) — it is
the single source of routing truth; never route from memory or to unlisted
slugs. Match **tone-first**:

- Lead with `mood`, `tone`, `occasion`, and `best_for` — match the *feeling*
the deck should have, not the industry. A confident editorial template can
carry a tech talk; a warm reflective one can carry a finance retro if that
is the taste the user signals.
- `avoid_for` is a soft warning, not a veto — if the user explicitly asks for
that look, the user wins.
- `formality` and `density` sanity-check against audience and content volume;
flag a genuine mismatch rather than silently obeying it.
- `scheme` is a hard signal only when the user asks for light or dark.
- When the user names a firm, brand, or style ("McKinsey", "NYT graphics",
"zine"), search **every** template's metadata for it before deciding.
Shortlist all honest matches and describe how they differ (e.g. classic
consulting idiom vs. its modern data-led sibling); synthesize a custom
theme only when nothing in the catalog genuinely matches.

Shortlist **two to four genuinely different candidates**: the obvious fit,
one alternative that reads warmer or quieter, and — when the brief has
latitude — one wildcard that reinterprets it.

Then clarify, always **before generating**:

- Use the clarification tool: recommended option first marked `Recommended`,
each option a human-readable name plus one sentence on its character.
Never expose bare slugs.
- If the request carries no tone signal at all, add one question in the same
clarification round asking about occasion and desired mood (e.g.
authoritative and analytical · warm and editorial · bold and design-led ·
playful). Re-route if the answer contradicts the shortlist.
- When candidates are visually far apart and the deck title is already
known, optionally build one-slide cover previews — full skeleton, one
cover per candidate, populated with the real title — and give the user
the file paths so they can compare looks directly.
- Skip the clarification only when the user explicitly names a template or a
style, or the request is an edit to an existing deck.

**Requested style not in the catalog?** If the user names an aesthetic, a
brand, a reference deck/site/screenshot, or answers the clarification with
free text the catalog cannot honestly serve, do not force the nearest
template. Read [references/custom-theme.md](references/custom-theme.md) and
synthesize a bespoke theme on the same substrate — same token contract, same
components, same validator. Offer to save a successful bespoke theme into
the catalog.

For an existing HTML deck, preserve its architecture and visual system; do not
migrate it to this substrate unless the user asks for a redesign.

### 3. Map the content

Read all supplied material. Inventory every important section, decision,
number, table, requirement, image, and speaker note, and map it to a slide
sequence that argues — situation before complication, evidence before
recommendation. Split content rather than dropping it or shrinking it.

Numbers come from the material, never from imagination. If the user supplies
no data for a claim, write the claim without a fabricated statistic, or ask.
Real source lines go in `Doc.init({source})` and slide footers.

For `.pptx`:

```bash
python3 scripts/extract-pptx.py input.pptx output-directory
```

Then read `output-directory/extracted-slides.json` and preserve source order,
content, images, and notes while redesigning. If the deck uses supplied
images, read [references/image-handling.md](references/image-handling.md)
first; never overwrite originals or repeat an image except a consistent logo.

### 4. Load the architecture

Always read, in full, before generating:

- [references/deck-template.md](references/deck-template.md) — file skeleton
and slide anatomy.
- [references/components.md](references/components.md) — component and chart
vocabulary.
- The one selected theme in `references/themes/<slug>.md` — tokens, grammar,
and working example slides.

Embed `assets/deck-core.css` and `assets/deck-core.js` verbatim. Copy the
theme CSS verbatim. The theme's example slides show the intended rhythm and
voice — adapt their structure, replace every word and number.

### 5. Write the slides

**Titles carry the argument.** Every content-slide title states a finding —
short, specific, usually with the number ("Two corridors carry the entire H1
volume gain"), never a topic label ("Volume analysis"). Read the titles alone
top to bottom: they must work as a complete summary of the deck. Sentence
case, no title case, no colons-with-subtitle constructions.

**One idea per slide.** The title makes the claim; the body is its evidence:
one chart, one table, one comparison, one worked example. If a slide needs two
ideas, it is two slides.

**Prefer components over bullets.** Numbers go in stat rows or KPI cards with
units and periods; comparisons in tables or paired panels; trends in charts;
processes in timelines or steps. When a list is genuinely right, four items or
fewer, each with a bold lead and a specific point. Never nest bullets.

**No filler slides.** No agenda, no "Thank you", no "Questions?", no
"Key takeaways" that restates titles. The closing slide does work: decision
requested, owners, dates, or the single number to remember.

**Write like a person who was there.** Concrete subjects and verbs; numbers
with units, periods, and comparators; the theme's voice (an audit clause, a
founder's TL;DR, a teacher's prompt read differently). Banned: "leverage",
"delve", "robust", "seamless", "cutting-edge", "holistic", "innovative
solutions", "in today's fast-paced world", "unlock", "empower", "journey",
adjective pairs like "clear and compelling", and any sentence that could
appear unchanged in someone else's deck.

### 6. Compose the slides

- Choose the chart by the question, not for variety's sake — but a deck whose
every exhibit is the same chart type is usually answering lazily; the
routing in `components.md` gives the mapping.
- Do not repeat the same body composition on consecutive slides; the theme's
grammar lists its patterns — rotate through them as the content allows.
- Fill honestly: a slide should use roughly two-thirds to nine-tenths of the
pad height. Too empty → merge or promote to a focus slide (`c-bignum`,
pullquote). Too full → split.
- Respect the canvas budget. A slide holds the title block plus **one** main
composition, plus at most one strip (stat row or insight banner). Two
stacked multi-row compositions — e.g. three callout rows *and* a panel
grid — will not fit the fixed 16:9 canvas; that is two slides. When in
doubt, split: the deck gains a slide, the audience loses nothing.
- `data-anim` on 3–6 major blocks per slide, not on every list item. One
`k-bgfx` texture at most, covers and dividers only.
- Color is meaning: the theme's accent marks the focal point; `--cat-*` in
order for series; semantic colors only for genuine good/bad. Never introduce
hex values in slide markup — use tokens.
- Every chart: `data-alt` sentence, declared unit, legend when multi-series,
source in the footer. Interactive extras (switcher, legend toggles,
sortable tables, count-ups) where they let the audience interrogate the
evidence, not as decoration.
- Deck-specific CSS is a last resort: under \~40 lines, token-derived sizes
only, and only for a component neither core nor theme provides.

### 7. Validate, fix, deliver

```bash
python3 scripts/validate-deck.py /path/to/deck.html
```

Fix every FAIL, then re-run until clean. Read every WARN and act on it unless
you have a stated reason not to — warnings encode the slop checklist
(topic-label titles, bullet-only slides, repeated compositions, missing
units/sources/alt text, banned phrases, filler slides).

Then inspect the source once more: all source content represented in order;
theme grammar followed; no leftover example text, ids, or sample numbers.

QA is source-first and must not require a browser. Use one only if already
available. For PDF, native Print → Save as PDF (slides print 1280×720).

Deliver the file path, selected template, slide count, and controls (Present
button, arrows/click/swipe, Esc). Open the HTML when the environment supports
it.

## Gotchas

- The core blocks are byte-sacred. If a behavior seems missing, you are
looking for a theme class or a `data-` attribute, not a core edit.
- `data-series` and `data-sets` are JSON in single-quoted attributes: double
quotes inside, no trailing commas, labels count matching values count.
- Charts size from `data-height` in 1000-per-sheet-width units; don't wrap
charts in fixed-height boxes.
- `sheet--invert`/`sheet--accent`/theme dark variants re-map tokens — check
the theme CSS before adding per-element colors on dark slides.
- Footers come from `data-foot` + `Doc.init`; don't hand-write footer text
into slides. Blank a slot with `data-r=""`, don't omit the footer element
(covers may drop it deliberately).
- No slide scrolls internally. No content is omitted to satisfy a slide
count. Split the slide instead.
- Slides are fixed canvases with `overflow:hidden` — content that doesn't
fit is silently clipped behind the footer. The runtime stamps any clipped
slide with a red "Overflow — split this slide" badge (review mode only).
A deck must never ship with that badge visible; fix by splitting, never by
shrinking type, padding, or chart heights.
- Keep the `k-bar` and present HUD exactly as the skeleton has them.

## Reference map

- [references/template-index.json](references/template-index.json) — routing
metadata for every template; the single source of routing truth.
- [references/deck-template.md](references/deck-template.md) — always read.
- [references/components.md](references/components.md) — always read.
- `references/themes/<slug>.md` — read exactly the selected one.
- [references/custom-theme.md](references/custom-theme.md) — read when
synthesizing a bespoke style the catalog lacks.
- [assets/deck-core.css](assets/deck-core.css),
[assets/deck-core.js](assets/deck-core.js) — embed verbatim, never edit.
- [scripts/extract-pptx.py](scripts/extract-pptx.py) — for `.pptx` input;
requires `python-pptx==1.0.2`.
- [scripts/validate-deck.py](scripts/validate-deck.py) — run on every deck;
Python standard library only.
- [scripts/validate-themes.py](scripts/validate-themes.py) — catalog linter;
run after adding or editing any theme file.
- [scripts/refresh-core.py](scripts/refresh-core.py) — re-embed current core
assets into an existing deck after a core update.
